Discussion
Principal findings
Athletic trainers are first responders to sports injuries and play an active role in the diagnosis, management,
and treatment of injury and illness [13]. The quality of these trainers can significantly impact a team's
success. Our analysis found no statistically significant correlation between NFLPA ratings of athletic
trainers and strength and conditioning coaches and the total number of injuries or weeks missed due to
injury. These findings indicate that higher subjective staff ratings were not associated with improved injury
outcomes at the team level.
Interpretation of findings
While no association was identified, this finding should be interpreted with caution. Given the ecological
study design, which relies on aggregated team-level data, the analysis is inherently limited in its ability to
detect individual-level relationships and is susceptible to confounding. As such, the absence of a significant
correlation does not necessarily indicate that no true relationship exists.
The subjective nature of player ratings may also contribute to this finding. Players may base evaluations on
personal experiences, such as communication style or interpersonal relationships, rather than objective
measures of treatment effectiveness. These factors may obscure any underlying association between staff
performance and injury outcomes. Future prospective studies focusing on individual-level data, particularly
among injury-prone athletes, may help clarify the long-term impact of staff interventions.
When considered in the context of the NFL, these ratings should not be used to infer the effectiveness of
training or rehabilitation programs in injury prevention or management. However, they may still provide
meaningful insight into player satisfaction and team environment.
Additionally, the use of the term “Training Staff” in the players’ evaluations could introduce errors in the
results. While this term was interpreted by the authors of this study to represent athletic trainers, the term
“training staff” may be construed by some individuals to include a number of other roles, potentially even
strength and conditioning coaches. If some players included strength and conditioning coaches in their
evaluation of training staff, this would cause a confounding bias in the comparisons made in this study.
Implications
Athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches should prioritize the standardization of training
protocols and emphasize evidence-based practices to enhance injury prevention and management. For
example, educating athletes and coaches on the limitations of certain protective equipment may reduce
preventable injuries [16]. Reducing variability in program design and increasing integration of sports science
and continuing education may improve the consistency and effectiveness of injury prevention strategies.
Future research
Future research should focus on developing objective and reliable methods to evaluate athletic trainers and
strength and conditioning coaches. Longitudinal studies utilizing individual-level player data will likely
provide a more accurate assessment of the relationship between staff performance and injury outcomes.
Additionally, further investigation into how staff implement evidence-based recommendations from sports
scientists may offer insight into optimizing injury prevention strategies [15].
Limitations
This study has several important limitations, the most critical of which is the potential for ecological fallacy.

Additionally, the analysis did not control for several important confounding variables that may influence
both staff ratings and injury rates, including player age and experience, team playing style, training
facilities, team practice and playing surface types, and environmental factors. Injury reports may also have
included absences unrelated to injury, such as illness or suspension, further confounding the results.
Another bias that may have influenced the results of this study is the likability bias, with some players
ranking more lenient trainers higher than those who are strictly evidence-based in their approach.
Finally, the retrospective nature of the study introduces the potential for selection and recall bias, which
may limit the validity of the findings [17].
Conclusions
There was no significant correlation between the NFLPA's subjective rankings of team athletic trainers or
strength and conditioning coaches and the total number of injuries sustained or the total number of weeks
players missed due to injury. While this finding is supported by near-zero R² values and non-significant p-
values, the interpretation of this result warrants caution. Given the ecological study design, which is
inherently limited in its ability to detect individual-level relationships and is susceptible to confounding,
the absence of a significant association at the aggregate level does not necessarily indicate that no true
relationship exists. Rather, this null finding may reflect methodological constraints, including ecological
fallacy and uncontrolled confounders, rather than the impact of these personnel on injury prevention and
recovery timelines. Although the NFLPA rankings may still provide value to players in assessing team
environment and satisfaction, further research using more robust, individual-level study designs is needed
to better evaluate the role of athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches in injury prevention
and recovery across both professional and amateur sports.

objective metrics that accurately capture their impact on athlete performance and development. This study
aims to assess the predictive value of the National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) rankings for
evaluating the effectiveness of athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches.
Methods
This study employed a cross-sectional ecological design. Data were collected from publicly available
databases to quantify the total number of injuries sustained by players on each National Football League
(NFL) team, the total number of weeks players missed due to injury on each team, and the overall rankings
for each team’s athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches in the 2024-2025 NFL regular
season. All data were collected, and Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were obtained. For each of the
coefficients obtained, significance was determined based on a sample size (n) of 32 and a significance value
() of 0.05.
Results
Over the course of the 2024-2025 NFL season, there were a total of 1,149 players who missed at least one
game due to injury during the regular season. This accounted for a total of 5,811 weeks missed. The league-
wide averages for the number of players who missed a game due to injury and cumulative weeks missed due
to injury were 36.097 and 183.645, respectively. NFLPA rankings for athletic trainers showed no meaningful
correlation with players who missed a game due to injury (ρ = -0.030) and total weeks missed due to injury
(ρ = -0.031). NFLPA rankings for strength and conditioning staff were weakly correlated with players who
missed a game due to injury (ρ = -0.267) and total weeks missed due to injury (ρ = -0.238).
Conclusion
There was no significant correlation between the NFLPA rankings for athletic trainers or strength and
conditioning coaches and the total number of injuries or total number of weeks missed for each team. While
this information can be valuable for players to assess how much other players value their team's trainers and
strength and conditioning staff, it offers little to no predictive value for the effectiveness of these programs
in preventing injuries and minimizing time missed.

Introduction
In the United States, the National Football League (NFL) is the most-watched sports league, with over 970
billion minutes watched across 284 televised games between 2022 and 2023 [1]. Professional football is a
multibillion-dollar-a-year industry, yet the total number of active players in the NFL each year is less than
2,000 [2]. There are a total of 32 NFL teams, and the total number of NFL players in each franchise is
trimmed yearly to an active gameday roster of 53 individuals [2]. Given the high value each of these players
provides to their respective teams each week, team owners and coaching staff are motivated to keep their
players on the field [3]. One of the most important ways a team can keep its players on the field is by
preventing injuries [4]. Injuries significantly impact the lives of athletes on and off the field, and the stakes
are even higher for professional athletes [5]. The NFL is aware of this, and efforts have been made in recent

A unique role employed by each of the NFL teams is that of athletic trainers. Athletic trainers play a crucial
role in the primary prevention of injuries and health promotion of athletes at both amateur and professional
levels, as well as supporting athletes on their road to recovery following an injury [7,8]. Each NFL team has
roughly four athletic trainers, which includes one head athletic trainer, one to two associate head athletic
trainers, and three assistants [9]. For athletic trainers to be successful, they must follow evidence-based
practices and utilize both communication and problem-solving skills to best care for their players [8,10]. It
has been demonstrated that athletic trainers can be a valuable yet cost-effective asset that helps both
prevent injuries and address the health needs of athletes [8,11]. Additionally, rehabilitation time and
performance following an injury have been shown to improve when athletic training interventions are
utilized; however, data are sparse on the best ways to evaluate athletic trainers prospectively in their ability
to treat their players effectively due to a lack of standardization across the field [8,11].
In addition to utilizing the services of athletic trainers, another way to help prevent injury in high-level
athletes is through the utilization of strength and conditioning programs. It has been shown that increasing
strength-training volume and intensity decreases the risk of sports-related injury [12]. This is especially true
for preventing overuse injury [13]. Additionally, once an athlete is injured, prior strength and conditioning
training has been shown to shorten recovery time and help athletes return to their sport sooner [13].
However, some studies have shown that excessive exercise can be a risk factor for developing overuse injury
in certain patient populations [14]. Given that strength and conditioning can both increase and decrease
injury risk in athletes, teams need to implement strategies that maximize the protective effects of exercise
while minimizing its deleterious effects.
One key individual utilized by NFL teams is the strength and conditioning coach. The role of these coaches
extends beyond improving the physical abilities of the athletes they train [14]. They are also responsible for
communicating with athletic trainers and other members of the coaching staff to both advocate for their
players and play a crucial role in the prevention of injuries [14]. These coaches work closely with athletic
trainers to help identify players who are at a higher risk of injury. They take steps to modify the athlete’s
workload with the hope of preventing an injury from taking them off the field entirely [14]. While these
coaches are in a unique position to help prevent injuries in these athletes, it has been shown that strength
and conditioning coaches may be hesitant to utilize evidence-based sports science recommendations and are
more likely to implement recommendations from peers or mentors [15].
As athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches can vary in their methods for helping athletes on
their team, it can be challenging to evaluate the quality of these coaches. While this may be less practical at
the amateur level, the NFL has attempted to evaluate these programs through a survey program. Every year,
the National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) administers an online census survey to the players
who were on a roster for a team in the NFL the previous year [14]. The purpose of this survey is to evaluate
workplace conditions and the overall perceived quality of the sports medicine staff for each NFL team to
both provide insight for potential players who might switch teams and to promote quality improvement of
the various teams in the NFL [14]. Each team is provided with a grade that can be compared to the other
teams in the league across 11 categories, including data about the teams’ athletic training staff and strength
coaches [14].
While the data collected from the NFL players in this survey provides insight into a team's perceived quality
of athletic trainers and strength coaches, it does not directly evaluate how well these trainers and coaches
implement evidence-based practices or the generalizability of their programs to other teams. Additionally,
these data do not explain to team management how effective their athletic trainers and strength and
conditioning coaches are at preventing injuries and getting players back to the game at an earlier time. This
is especially important to consider for NFL players because injuries lead to lost wages, and it is also vital for
teams as injuries may contribute to a loss in the league standings column [14].
While this tool does not directly evaluate the methods implemented by athletic trainers and strength and
conditioning coaches, it may still give players an idea of the overall quality of the athletic training and
strength and conditioning staff. The purpose of this study is to determine if there is a correlation between a
team's ranking in the NFLPA survey and the injuries sustained by players on their respective teams. We
hypothesize that a better team ranking in strength and conditioning coaches and athletic training staff will
be associated with lower injury rates and less total game time missed, providing valuable insights to players,
coaches, team ownership, and fans of the NFL.

Discussion
Principal findings
Athletic trainers are first responders to sports injuries and play an active role in the diagnosis, management,
and treatment of injury and illness [13]. The quality of these trainers can significantly impact a team's
success. Our analysis found no statistically significant correlation between NFLPA ratings of athletic
trainers and strength and conditioning coaches and the total number of injuries or weeks missed due to
injury. These findings indicate that higher subjective staff ratings were not associated with improved injury
outcomes at the team level.
Interpretation of findings
While no association was identified, this finding should be interpreted with caution. Given the ecological
study design, which relies on aggregated team-level data, the analysis is inherently limited in its ability to
detect individual-level relationships and is susceptible to confounding. As such, the absence of a significant
correlation does not necessarily indicate that no true relationship exists.
The subjective nature of player ratings may also contribute to this finding. Players may base evaluations on
personal experiences, such as communication style or interpersonal relationships, rather than objective
measures of treatment effectiveness. These factors may obscure any underlying association between staff
performance and injury outcomes. Future prospective studies focusing on individual-level data, particularly
among injury-prone athletes, may help clarify the long-term impact of staff interventions.
When considered in the context of the NFL, these ratings should not be used to infer the effectiveness of
training or rehabilitation programs in injury prevention or management. However, they may still provide
meaningful insight into player satisfaction and team environment.
Additionally, the use of the term “Training Staff” in the players’ evaluations could introduce errors in the
results. While this term was interpreted by the authors of this study to represent athletic trainers, the term
“training staff” may be construed by some individuals to include a number of other roles, potentially even
strength and conditioning coaches. If some players included strength and conditioning coaches in their
evaluation of training staff, this would cause a confounding bias in the comparisons made in this study.
Implications
Athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches should prioritize the standardization of training
protocols and emphasize evidence-based practices to enhance injury prevention and management. For
example, educating athletes and coaches on the limitations of certain protective equipment may reduce
preventable injuries [16]. Reducing variability in program design and increasing integration of sports science
and continuing education may improve the consistency and effectiveness of injury prevention strategies.
Future research
Future research should focus on developing objective and reliable methods to evaluate athletic trainers and
strength and conditioning coaches. Longitudinal studies utilizing individual-level player data will likely
provide a more accurate assessment of the relationship between staff performance and injury outcomes.
Additionally, further investigation into how staff implement evidence-based recommendations from sports
scientists may offer insight into optimizing injury prevention strategies [15].
Limitations
This study has several important limitations, the most critical of which is the potential for ecological fallacy.

Conclusions
There was no significant correlation between the NFLPA's subjective rankings of team athletic trainers or
strength and conditioning coaches and the total number of injuries sustained or the total number of weeks
players missed due to injury. While this finding is supported by near-zero R² values and non-significant p-
values, the interpretation of this result warrants caution. Given the ecological study design, which is
inherently limited in its ability to detect individual-level relationships and is susceptible to confounding,
the absence of a significant association at the aggregate level does not necessarily indicate that no true
relationship exists. Rather, this null finding may reflect methodological constraints, including ecological
fallacy and uncontrolled confounders, rather than the impact of these personnel on injury prevention and
recovery timelines. Although the NFLPA rankings may still provide value to players in assessing team
environment and satisfaction, further research using more robust, individual-level study designs is needed
to better evaluate the role of athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches in injury prevention
and recovery across both professional and amateur sports.

# Davidson et al. 2026: NFLPA Ratings and Player Injuries

> **Citation**
> Davidson R, Gordon S, Hussain A, et al. (June 15, 2026) An Analysis of the Association Between National Football League Players Association (NFLPA) Ratings and Player Injuries. Cureus 18(6): e110909. DOI 10.7759/cureus.110909 `[p. 1]`
>
> Full author list in the Zotero record: Robert Davidson, Sean Gordon, Abraham Hussain, Scarlett Schneider. Year is printed as 2026 (published 06/15/2026) `[p. 1]`. Journal name and volume are printed in the citation line `[p. 1]`.

## Why it was promoted

Not printed in the text. The Zotero record places the item in the "SecondBrain Queue" collection, which is the only promotion signal available. The topic is whether staff quality ratings (NFLPA rankings for athletic trainers and strength and conditioning coaches) track injury outcomes `[p. 2]`. The paper frames this as an attempt to judge staff effectiveness with objective metrics, which the authors say is hard to do `[p. 1]`.

## Research question

Whether a team's NFLPA ranking for its athletic training staff and for its strength and conditioning staff correlates with the team's injury burden in the 2024-2025 NFL regular season `[p. 2-3]`. The authors hypothesised that better rankings would go with fewer injuries and less time missed `[p. 2]`.

## Population and context

- Participants: 32 NFL teams, analysed as team-level units. The unit of analysis is the team, not the player `[p. 3]`. The 1,149 players who missed at least one game are the aggregated injury count, not study participants with individual data `[p. 1]`.
- Sport and level: National Football League, professional level. Methods give the 2024-2025 regular season `[p. 1, p. 3]`. The Figure 1 caption says "2024 season" `[p. 4]`.
- Training or return-to-play context: Injury burden from the regular season injury report. Ratings come from an anonymous annual survey of players on NFL rosters `[p. 2-3]`.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Players listed on the injury report who did not miss a game were excluded from the game-missed count. Injury report entries where the player took part in the game were excluded from the weeks-missed count `[p. 3]`. Injury report statuses counted were probable, questionable, doubtful, out, physically unable to perform, and injured reserve `[p. 3]`. The number of survey respondents is not printed.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Cross-sectional ecological correlation study, team level, n = 32 `[p. 2-3]`. Retrospective `[p. 6]`.
- Exposure or intervention: Not an intervention. Exposure is the NFLPA team ranking for "Training Staff" and for "Strength coaches", where rank 1 is the best and rank 32 the worst `[p. 3]`.
- Comparator: None. The analysis is a correlation between the ranking and each outcome across the 32 teams `[p. 3]`.

# Thomas et al. 2015: Maximum Isometric Strength and Vertical Jump Performance

> **Citation**
> Thomas C, Jones PA, Rothwell J, Chiang CY, Comfort P. An investigation into the relationship between maximum isometric strength and vertical jump performance. J Strength Cond Res 29(8): 2176-2185, 2015. `[p. 1]` Month (August 2015) is printed in the page header `[p. 2]`. The DOI is not printed in the text; it comes from the Zotero record (10.1519/JSC.0000000000000866).

## Why it was promoted

Not printed in the text. The Zotero record places the item in the "SecondBrain Queue" collection, which is the only promotion signal available. The paper addresses how isometric strength tests (isometric midthigh pull) relate to jump performance in athletes, a common choice for strength and power testing batteries `[p. 2]`.

## Research question

The aim was to determine the relationship between maximal isometric strength variables (isometric peak force, maximum rate of force development, impulse at 100, 200 and 300 ms, and total impulse) and vertical jump performance (squat jump and countermovement jump: peak velocity, peak force, peak power and jump height). The authors also asked whether athletes strong on the isometric test would also perform well on the jump measures `[p. 2]`.

## Population and context

- Participants: 22 male collegiate athletes, active in cricket, judo, rugby and soccer. Volunteers took part as part of normal training and monitoring `[p. 2]`. Age 21.3 +/- 2.9 years, height 175.63 +/- 8.23 cm, body mass 78.06 +/- 10.77 kg (mean +/- SD) `[p. 1]`.
- Sport and level: Collegiate (university-level) athletes from several team and individual sports `[p. 2, p. 8]`.
- Training or return-to-play context: Not an injury or rehabilitation sample. Athletes were asked to avoid training for 48 hours before testing and to keep fluid and diet consistent `[p. 2]`.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Not printed beyond the sport mix, male sex and the 48-hour training abstinence. Ethics approval and written informed consent are reported `[p. 2]`. The inclusion criteria for the sample are not printed.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with one set of tests per athlete. A subgroup comparison split athletes by relative strength `[p. 2, p. 6]`. The number of test sessions and the time between them are not printed beyond the 10-minute rest between the jump tests and the isometric test `[p. 4]`.
- Exposure or intervention: Isometric midthigh pull (IMTP) on a portable force plate sampling at 600 Hz. Measures: isometric peak force (IPF), maximum rate of force development (mRFD), and impulse at 100, 200, 300 ms and total `[p. 4-5]`. No intervention was given.
- Comparator: Relative strength groups. Athletes were ranked by relative IPF (IPF divided by body mass). The strongest 11 and weakest 11 were compared `[p. 6]`.
- Measurements and outcomes: Squat jump (SJ) and countermovement jump (CMJ) peak velocity, peak force, peak power and jump height, from force-plate data. Jump height was calculated from flight time `[p. 3-4]`. Each jump type had three trials `[p. 3]`.
- Analysis: Pearson product-moment correlations, interpreted with the Hopkins scale (small 0.1-0.29, moderate 0.30-0.49, large 0.50-0.69, very large 0.70-0.89) and a significance level of p <= 0.05 `[p. 6-7]`. Two-tailed independent t-tests and Cohen's d for the strong and weak groups `[p. 6]`. Reliability was assessed with ICC, %CV, typical error and change in mean `[p. 5]`.

## Key findings

All correlations are between athletes at one time point. No change within athletes over time was measured. The results show association, not cause.

- Absolute impulse measures from the IMTP (I100, I200, I300 and total impulse) were significantly correlated with jump peak force and peak power. Correlations ranged from r = 0.43 to 0.64 for peak force and r = 0.38 to 0.60 for peak power `[Table 3, p. 4]` `[p. 1]`.
  - I100 vs CMJ peak force: r = 0.64 (p <= 0.01). vs SJ peak force: r = 0.57 (p <= 0.01). vs CMJ peak power: r = 0.51 (p <= 0.05). vs SJ peak power: r = 0.60 (p <= 0.01) `[Table 3, p. 4]`.
  - Total impulse vs CMJ peak force: r = 0.43 and vs SJ peak force: r = 0.50 (both p <= 0.05). Total impulse vs SJ peak power: r = 0.38, not significant `[Table 3, p. 4]`.
- Absolute IPF was significantly correlated with CMJ peak force (r = 0.45, p <= 0.05) and SJ peak power (r = 0.46, p <= 0.05). Its correlations with SJ peak force (r = 0.41) and CMJ peak power (r = 0.34) were not significant `[Table 3, p. 4]`.
- Absolute IMTP measures were not significantly correlated with peak velocity or jump height in either jump. Correlation coefficients for these outcomes were between -0.30 and 0.13, none marked significant `[Table 3, p. 4]` `[p. 7]`.
- Absolute mRFD was not significantly correlated with any jump variable `[Table 3, p. 4]`. Its reliability was poor: %CV 15.1 (90% CI 12.0-20.9) `[Table 2, p. 4]`.
- Relative (per kg) IMTP measures were not significantly correlated with any jump variable `[Table 3, p. 4]`.
- Strong vs weak group (n = 11 each, split by relative IPF): relative IPF was 38.72 +/- 2.08 vs 30.40 +/- 4.01 N/kg, p = 0.01, Cohen's d = 2.60. Relative mRFD was 172.59 +/- 37.64 vs 103.12 +/- 35.95 N/kg/s, p = 0.01, d = 1.89 `[Table 7, p. 6]` `[p. 7]`.
- The same groups did not differ on jump outcomes. CMJ height was 0.33 +/- 0.05 vs 0.36 +/- 0.05 m (p = 0.19). SJ height was 0.29 +/- 0.06 vs 0.33 +/- 0.05 m (p = 0.14). No jump peak velocity, peak force or peak power difference was significant `[Table 7, p. 6]` `[p. 7]`.
- Reliability (ICC, 90% CI): IPF 0.97 (0.94-0.99), CV 4.2%. CMJ height 0.91, CV 5.1%. SJ height 0.86, CV 6.8%. mRFD 0.81, CV 15.1% `[Table 2, p. 4]`.
- Authors' conclusion: absolute isometric impulse and peak force relate to jump peak force and peak power, but not to jump height. Stronger athletes (by relative strength) did not jump higher than weaker athletes `[p. 1]` `[p. 8]`.

## Limitations and applicability

- Limitations reported by the authors:
  - The group may be homogeneous, which may limit findings `[p. 8]`.
  - Jump height from flight time may be limited by body position at take-off and landing. Jump-and-reach devices are less valid than force plates `[p. 7]`.
  - Relative and absolute measures were normalised differently (ratio scaling here, allometric scaling in some prior work), which may affect comparisons `[p. 8]`.
  - mRFD had a high %CV (15.1), so its reliability is uncertain `[p. 8]`.
  - Normative values for relative IMTP force-time measures are not established `[p. 8]`.
  - Unknown whether relative isometric findings transfer to dynamic strength such as 1RM back squat in this sample `[p. 8]`.
- Additional transfer limitations (interpretation, not author claims):
  - Sample size is 22 in total and 11 per subgroup. Confidence intervals for the correlations are not printed, so the precision of each r is not shown.
  - No sample size calculation is printed `[p. 2-7]`.
  - Athletes were male collegiate athletes from mixed sports. Results may not carry to women, elite athletes or single-sport squads.
  - Correlations are cross-sectional. They cannot show that raising isometric impulse would raise jump force or power.
- Reporting issues found on checking the text (this brief's check, not the authors' claims):
  - Abstract effect sizes for jump height (CMJ d = -0.29, SJ d = -0.34) do not match Table 7 (CMJ d = -0.60, SJ d = -0.72) `[p. 1]` `[Table 7, p. 6]`.
  - Weak-group body mass is 75.95 kg in the Results text `[p. 7]` but 75.98 kg in Table 7 `[p. 6]`.
  - Table numbers in the text do not match the printed tables. Results cite Table 2 for IMTP-CMJ correlations (Table 2 is reliability) and Table 4 for the group comparison (printed as Table 7) `[p. 7]`.
  - Discussion says stronger athletes "produced greater CMJ PF" `[p. 8]`. Table 7 shows 26.95 vs 26.84 N/kg with p = 0.96, which is not a meaningful difference `[Table 7, p. 6]`.

## Practitioner interpretation

Interpretation, not a study finding: In these collegiate athletes, absolute impulse from an isometric midthigh pull tracked how much force and power athletes produced in a jump. It did not track how high they jumped. So an isometric test may be a reasonable read on jump force and power, but the paper does not show that it predicts jump height. Relative strength (strength per kg) did not separate jump performance here, even though it separated the strong and weak groups on isometric measures. Staff should not read this as "stronger athletes jump higher". The authors suggest choosing tests that match the force and power demands of the sport, and developing these qualities in a periodised way `[p. 9]`. Any use with other squads should keep the population, the one-time design and the wide uncertainty in mind.

## Evidence map

|---|---|---|
| 22 male collegiate athletes; age, height, mass | `[p. 1]` `[p. 2]` | method |
| Absolute I100 vs CMJ peak force r = 0.64 (p <= 0.01) | `[Table 3, p. 4]` | result |
| Absolute IPF vs CMJ peak force r = 0.45; vs SJ peak power r = 0.46 | `[Table 3, p. 4]` | result |
| No significant IMTP correlation with jump height or peak velocity | `[Table 3, p. 4]` `[p. 7]` | result |
| Relative IMTP measures not significantly correlated with jumps | `[Table 3, p. 4]` | result |
| Strong vs weak groups differ on relative IPF (p = 0.01) and mRFD (p = 0.01) | `[Table 7, p. 6]` | result |
| Strong vs weak groups do not differ on jump height (p = 0.19 CMJ, p = 0.14 SJ) | `[Table 7, p. 6]` | result |
| mRFD %CV 15.1 limits reliability | `[Table 2, p. 4]` `[p. 8]` | limitation |
| Homogeneous sample; flight-time jump height; scaling choice | `[p. 7-8]` | limitation |
| Abstract effect sizes differ from Table 7 | `[p. 1]` `[Table 7, p. 6]` | limitation (reporting) |

tion, RFD) are required for the appropriate application of test-
ing results to formulate future resistance training program. The
2 most commonly used exercises for isometric strength assess-
ment are the isometric back squat and isometric midthigh pull
(IMTP) (15). Early research suggests IPF to correlate well with
VJ variables (r = 0.53–0.82), such as PF, PP, and jump height in
a range of populations such as weightlifting, cycling, recrea-
tionally trained, wrestling, American football, and soccer,
because of similarities in vertically directed force production
and the subsequent biomechanically derived variables. This
indicates that the IMTP may be a valid predictor of VJ per-
formance in a variety of athletes and sports (15,19,32).
During the IMTP, a standardized pulling technique has
not been determined, with some researchers using a pull
from just above the knee and others using a midthigh pull
(14,15,19,26,33). Taking this into account, a recent study
proposed that knee and hip angles be self-selected by ath-
letes in order for each individual to position themselves in an
optimal body position, with the bar at midthigh, replicating
the midthigh pull position to produce the highest PF possi-
ble (33).
Another common strength measurement during the
IMTP is RFD, which has not been as consistent in terms
of its reliability and relationship to dynamic performance.
Early investigations found RFD to show small to very large
signiﬁcant correlations (r = 20.18 to 0.82) with VJ perfor-
mance when using a sampling window of 2 milliseconds.
The results of Haff et al. (14) have been questioned with
small nonsigniﬁcant correlations observed between RFD
and VJ performance (r = 20.04 to 20.34) but very large

RFD and VJ PP in elite female weightlifters (r = 0.88–

of change between 2 adjacent force samples divided by the

found small to large nonsigniﬁcant correlations, whereas
Stone et al. (32) only observed moderate inverse correlations
between RFD with sprint cycling performance variables (r =

study by Beckham et al. (3), RFD was determined using
a 5-millisecond window in addition to 100-, 150-, 200-,
and 250-millisecond time points, with 0–200 milliseconds
observing large signiﬁcant correlations (r = 0.58–0.65) and
0–250 milliseconds large to very large signiﬁcant correlations
with weightlifting performances (r = 0.58–0.78). Kraska et al.
(20) found RFD to show high reliability when sampling at
10-millisecond windows, showing moderate signiﬁcant cor-
relations (r = 0.43–0.48) to VJ height, and these correlations
were extended to large correlations (r . 0.50) when mea-
sured with weighted VJ performance at 20 kg. Although
outside the scope of this investigation, the question remains
whether IMTP RFD be determined through a sampling
window (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 20 ms) or a speciﬁc time window
(e.g., 0–50, 0–100, 0–150, and 0–200 ms).
The aim of this study was to determine the relationship
between maximal isometric strength variables and measure-
ments of VJ performance, in collegiate athletes. In addition,
observations were made to discover whether those athletes
who have high performance in isometric strength testing
would have high performance in VJ performance measures.
It was hypothesized that relationships between maximal
isometric strength variables and VJ performance measures
would be similar to those previously identiﬁed in a similar
subject cohort (20,23). In addition, we hypothesized that
relatively stronger athletes will perform better in VJ perfor-
mance measures, speciﬁcally VJ PP and VJ height.
METHODS
Experimental Approach to the Problem
This study was designed to investigate the relationships
between isometric strength (IPF, maximum rate of force
development [mRFD], IMP100, I200, I300, and total IMP)
and maximal VJ performance (SJ and CMJ PV, PF, PP, and
jump height) in collegiate athletes. Maximal isometric
strength was selected as it is highly reliable and provides
very efﬁcient measures of maximal strength in a variety of
populations (15,23,24), whereas SJ and CMJ were selected as
these are commonly used to assess VJ performance (26,39).
Athletes were required to abstain from training for 48
hours before testing and asked to maintain a consistent ﬂuid
and dietary intake on each day of testing. Before the start of
testing, athletes were instructed to perform a standardized
warm-up, as directed by the investigator.
Subjects
Twenty-two collegiate male athletes (mean 6 SD; age =
21.3 6 2.9 years; height = 175.63 6 8.23 cm; body mass =
78.06 6 10.77 kg) active in cricket, judo, rugby, and soccer
participated in this investigation. All individuals volunteered
for the testing as part of their normal training and monitor-
ing regime. Ethical approval was provided by the institu-
tional review board, and all athletes provided written
informed consent. All procedures conformed to the Decla-
ration of Helsinki. All individuals were familiar with testing
protocols.

correlations existed. Isometric midthigh pull I100, I200,
I300, and total IMP showed moderate to large signiﬁcant
correlations (p # 0.05) with CMJ PF. Isometric midthigh

Differences between relatively strong athlete and weak
athlete group mean values are presented in Table 4. The
strong group had a greater body mass than the weak group
(strong = 80.13 6 8.28 kg; weak = 75.95 6 12.88 kg). Sta-
tistically signiﬁcant differences (p # 0.01) were found
between groups on relative IPF and relative IMTP RFD,

relative SJ PF, and relative SJ PP, between stronger and
weaker athletes.
There was no statistical difference in CMJ PV, SJ PV,
relative CMJ PP, CMJ height, and SJ height between
stronger and weaker athletes (Tables 5–7).
DISCUSSION
The aims of this study were to determine the relationships
between maximal isometric strength variables and measure-
ments of VJ performance and establish whether athletes who
have high performance in isometric strength testing would
have high performance in VJ performance measures. Our
results suggest that absolute measures of IMTP strength,
speciﬁcally IMP generated in #300 milliseconds, best corre-
late with PF and PP measures of VJ performance. In contrast
to previous research (20,32), we have found that athletes
who have signiﬁcantly greater relative isometric strength
levels jump the same height as those with lower relative
isometric strength values.
Absolute IMTP performance measures do not signiﬁ-
cantly correlate with performance variables in the VJ such as
PV and jump height; however, they do correlate with VJ PF
and PP. Additionally, it seems that when comparing iso-

(14,15,26) but opposite to studies that found signiﬁcant cor-

was determined from ﬂight time, which may be limited by

    "text": "AN INVESTIGATION INTO THE RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN
MAXIMUM ISOMETRIC STRENGTH AND VERTICAL
JUMP PERFORMANCE
CHRISTOPHER THOMAS,1 PAUL A. JONES,1 JAMES ROTHWELL,1 CHIEH Y. CHIANG,2
AND PAUL COMFORT1
1Directorate of Sport, Exercise and Physiotherapy, University of Salford, Salford, Greater Manchester, United Kingdom; and
2Department of Exercise and Sport Science, East Tennessee State University, Johnson City, Tennessee
ABSTRACT
Thomas, C, Jones, PA, Rothwell, J, Chiang, CY, and Comfort, P.
An investigation into the relationship between maximum iso-
metric strength and vertical jump performance. J Strength Cond
Res 29(8): 2176–2185, 2015—Research has demonstrated
a clear relationship between dynamic strength and vertical jump
(VJ) performance; however, the relationship of isometric strength
and VJ performance has been studied less extensively. The aim
of this study was to determine the relationship between isomet-
ric strength and performance during the squat jump (SJ) and
countermovement jump (CMJ). Twenty-two male collegiate ath-
letes (mean 6 SD; age = 21.3 6 2.9 years; height = 175.63 6
8.23 cm; body mass = 78.06 6 10.77 kg) performed isometric
midthigh
pulls
(IMTPs)
to
assess
isometric
peak
force
(IPF), maximum rate of force development, and impulse (IMP)
(I100, I200, and I300). Force-time data, collected during the VJs,
were used to calculate peak velocity, peak force (PF), peak
power (PP), and jump height. Absolute IMTP measures of IMP
showed the strongest correlations with VJ PF (r = 0.43–0.64;
p # 0.05) and VJ PP (r = 0.38–0.60; p # 0.05). No statistical
difference was observed in CMJ height (0.33 6 0.05 m vs. 0.36
6 0.05 m; p = 0.19; ES = –0.29) and SJ height performance
(0.29 6 0.06 m vs. 0.33 6 0.05 m; p = 0.14; ES = –0.34) when
comparing stronger to weaker athletes. The results of this study
illustrate that absolute IPF and IMP are related to VJ PF and PP
but not VJ height. Because stronger athletes did not jump higher
than weaker athletes, dynamic strength tests may be more prac-
tical methods of assessing the relationships between relative
strength levels and dynamic performance in collegiate athletes.
KEY WORDS peak force, peak power, jump height
INTRODUCTION
A
number of studies have investigated the relation-
ship between vertical jump performance (VJ),
both in the squat jump (SJ) and countermove-
ment jump (CMJ) to strength and power in
single-joint isometric tests (2), multijoint isometric tests
(14,15), and multijoint dynamic tests (40). Several of the
characteristics associated with strength (peak force [PF], rate
of force development [RFD], peak velocity [PV], and peak
power [PP]) have been identiﬁed as underlying mechanisms
related to sports performance, particularly in the VJ (30).
Success in sport depends on the development of force,
power, and impulse (IMP), all of which contribute to VJ
performance (2,24,30,38,40). Previous research reported VJ
to be a reliable predictor of success in a number of sports,
which include ice hockey (4), soccer (39), handball (5), vol-
leyball (28), rugby (13), karate (27), and weightlifting (34).
Strong correlations have been found between the 1 repeti-
tion maximum (RM) squat (7), isometric peak force (IPF)
(31), and PP during the CMJ and SJ (30). Furthermore,
training-induced increases in measures of maximum strength
have been shown to result in VJ height and power output
increases (30).
Studies have used various methods to assess strength
including isokinetics (42), machine squats (41), and free-
weight squats (26,31) when investigating the relationship
between strength and VJ performance. Moderate to strong
correlations (r = 0.54–0.94) have been observed between
free-weight squats and VJ performance (30,39). There can
be several explanations for the variations in strength of the
relationship between dynamic strength assessment and VJ
performance, and these include the method of strength test,
scaling of results, determination of VJ performance, and the
instruction of the VJ (24). Researchers involved in the testing
of lower-body strength have gravitated more toward the
traditional free-weight test of maximal strength as typically
used in assessing athletes in rugby union (1), American foot-
ball (12), soccer (39), and volleyball (29). More recently,
researchers have started to use variations of the power clean
to assess lower-body strength as these exercises have similar

    "text": "characteristics to sporting movements (sprinting, jumping,
change of direction [COD]) (18). As a result, weightlifting
exercises have been used as a method to test lower-body
strength and power among athletes competing in a range
of sports (14,18).
Previous literature indicates that isometric measures of
maximum strength have only weak-to-moderate correlations
with dynamic exercise variables (38). Isometric and dynamic
performance assessment differ in biomechanical characteristics
such as the type of loading, magnitude of loading, joint ranges
of motion, and joint angular velocities, resulting in some
training-induced adaptations being reﬂected in some tests
but not others (15,26,32). That is, testing methods that share
characteristics of sports performance (e.g., forces, body posi-
tion, RFD) are required for the appropriate application of test-
ing results to formulate future resistance training program. The
2 most commonly used exercises for isometric strength assess-
ment are the isometric back squat and isometric midthigh pull
(IMTP) (15). Early research suggests IPF to correlate well with
VJ variables (r = 0.53–0.82), such as PF, PP, and jump height in
a range of populations such as weightlifting, cycling, recrea-
tionally trained, wrestling, American football, and soccer,
because of similarities in vertically directed force production
and the subsequent biomechanically derived variables. This
indicates that the IMTP may be a valid predictor of VJ per-
formance in a variety of athletes and sports (15,19,32).
During the IMTP, a standardized pulling technique has
not been determined, with some researchers using a pull
from just above the knee and others using a midthigh pull
(14,15,19,26,33). Taking this into account, a recent study
proposed that knee and hip angles be self-selected by ath-
letes in order for each individual to position themselves in an
optimal body position, with the bar at midthigh, replicating
the midthigh pull position to produce the highest PF possi-
ble (33).
Another common strength measurement during the
IMTP is RFD, which has not been as consistent in terms
of its reliability and relationship to dynamic performance.
Early investigations found RFD to show small to very large
signiﬁcant correlations (r = 20.18 to 0.82) with VJ perfor-
mance when using a sampling window of 2 milliseconds.
The results of Haff et al. (14) have been questioned with
small nonsigniﬁcant correlations observed between RFD
and VJ performance (r = 20.04 to 20.34) but very large
and
nearly
perfect
signiﬁcant
correlations
between
RFD and VJ PP in elite female weightlifters (r = 0.88–
0.92), when calculating RFD as the peak RFD through rate
of change between 2 adjacent force samples divided by the
intersample time interval (2 milliseconds). Haff et al. (15)
found small to large nonsigniﬁcant correlations, whereas
Stone et al. (32) only observed moderate inverse correlations
between RFD with sprint cycling performance variables (r =
20.28 to 20.39) when using previously established RFD
analysis using a 5-millisecond window (31). In a recent
study by Beckham et al. (3), RFD was determined using
a 5-millisecond window in addition to 100-, 150-, 200-,
and 250-millisecond time points, with 0–200 milliseconds
observing large signiﬁcant correlations (r = 0.58–0.65) and
0–250 milliseconds large to very large signiﬁcant correlations
with weightlifting performances (r = 0.58–0.78). Kraska et al.
(20) found RFD to show high reliability when sampling at
10-millisecond windows, showing moderate signiﬁcant cor-
relations (r = 0.43–0.48) to VJ height, and these correlations
were extended to large correlations (r . 0.50) when mea-
sured with weighted VJ performance at 20 kg. Although
outside the scope of this investigation, the question remains
whether IMTP RFD be determined through a sampling
window (e.g., 2, 5, 10, 20 ms) or a speciﬁc time window
(e.g., 0–50, 0–100, 0–150, and 0–200 ms).
The aim of this study was to determine the relationship
between maximal isometric strength variables and measure-
ments of VJ performance, in collegiate athletes. In addition,
observations were made to discover whether those athletes
who have high performance in isometric strength testing
would have high performance in VJ performance measures.
It was hypothesized that relationships between maximal
isometric strength variables and VJ performance measures
would be similar to those previously identiﬁed in a similar
subject cohort (20,23). In addition, we hypothesized that
relatively stronger athletes will perform better in VJ perfor-
mance measures, speciﬁcally VJ PP and VJ height.
METHODS
Experimental Approach to the Problem
This study was designed to investigate the relationships
between isometric strength (IPF, maximum rate of force
development [mRFD], IMP100, I200, I300, and total IMP)
and maximal VJ performance (SJ and CMJ PV, PF, PP, and
jump height) in collegiate athletes. Maximal isometric
strength was selected as it is highly reliable and provides
very efﬁcient measures of maximal strength in a variety of
populations (15,23,24), whereas SJ and CMJ were selected as
these are commonly used to assess VJ performance (26,39).
Athletes were required to abstain from training for 48
hours before testing and asked to maintain a consistent ﬂuid
and dietary intake on each day of testing. Before the start of
testing, athletes were instructed to perform a standardized
warm-up, as directed by the investigator.
Subjects
Twenty-two collegiate male athletes (mean 6 SD; age =
21.3 6 2.9 years; height = 175.63 6 8.23 cm; body mass =
78.06 6 10.77 kg) active in cricket, judo, rugby, and soccer
participated in this investigation. All individuals volunteered
for the testing as part of their normal training and monitor-
ing regime. Ethical approval was provided by the institu-
tional review board, and all athletes provided written
informed consent. All procedures conformed to the Decla-
ration of Helsinki. All individuals were familiar with testing
protocols.

lines: ## Study design and methods

-- Design: Cross-sectional correlational study with one set of tests per athlete. A subgroup comparison split athletes by relative strength `[p. 2, p. 6]`. The number of test sessions and the time between them are not printed beyond the 10-minute rest between the jump tests and the isometric test `[p. 4]`.

+- Design: Cross-sectional correlational study. A subgroup comparison split athletes by relative strength `[p. 2, p. 6]`. The number of test sessions and the time between them are not printed beyond the 10-minute rest between the jump tests and the isometric test `[p. 4]`.

- Exposure or intervention: Isometric midthigh pull (IMTP) on a portable force plate sampling at 600 Hz. Measures: isometric peak force (IPF), maximum rate of force development (mRFD), and impulse at 100, 200, 300 ms and total `[p. 4-5]`. No intervention was given.
- Comparator: Relative strength groups. Athletes were ranked by relative IPF (IPF divided by body mass). The strongest 11 and weakest 11 were compared `[p. 6]`.

- Measurements and outcomes: Squat jump (SJ) and countermovement jump (CMJ) peak velocity, peak force, peak power and jump height, from force-plate data. Jump height was calculated from flight time `[p. 3-4]`. Each jump type had three trials `[p. 3]`.

lines: ## Practitioner interpretation

-Interpretation, not a study finding: In these collegiate athletes, absolute impulse from an isometric midthigh pull tracked how much force and power athletes produced in a jump. It did not track how high they jumped. So an isometric test may be a reasonable read on jump force and power, but the paper does not show that it predicts jump height. Relative strength (strength per kg) did not separate jump performance here, even though it separated the strong and weak groups on isometric measures. Staff should not read this as "stronger athletes jump higher". The authors suggest choosing tests that match the force and power demands of the sport, and developing these qualities in a periodised way `[p. 9]`. Any use with other squads should keep the population, the one-time design and the wide uncertainty in mind.

Weak-group mass 75.95 (p. 7) vs 75.98 (Table 7). Table numbering errors in Results. Discussion's "greater CMJ PF" (26.95 vs 26.84, p = 0.96).

Changes made
1. Frontmatter doi: was 10.1519/JSC.0000000000000866. The DOI is not printed anywhere in the text (the brief itself says so). Now doi: "" per the rule. The citation note that the DOI exists in Zotero is kept.
2. Study design: removed "with one set of tests per athlete". Not printed, and the text implies repeated measurement (reliability ICC/change in mean, "on each day of testing", p. 2, p. 5).
3. Key findings, first bullet: said all four absolute impulse measures were significantly correlated with jump peak power. Total impulse vs SJ peak power (r = 0.38) is not significant in Table 3 (p. 4). Now says "except total impulse vs SJ peak power".
4. Limitations: "Relative and absolute measures were normalised differently" was wrong. The text (p. 8) says this study used ratio scaling while Kraska and Stone used allometric scaling, offered as a possible reason relative impulse did not correlate. Rewritten to say that.
5. Reporting issues: added that the abstract's peak power range r = 0.38-0.60 is labelled p <= 0.05, but 0.38 is not significant in Table 3 (p. 1, p. 4).
6. Practitioner interpretation: the authors' recommendation was paraphrased as "choose tests that match the force and power demands of the sport", which p. 9 does not say. Now: consider force, RFD, power and impulse, plus validity and reliability, when building testing protocols, and develop them in a periodised way (p. 9).

Residual concerns for Eric
- Strong vs weak groups were formed on relative IPF, so their large IPF difference (d = 2.60) is built into the split, not a finding.
- Table 7 prints p = 0.01 for IPF and mRFD; with d = 2.60 and 1.89 at n = 11 per group the true p is much smaller, so "0.01" is likely a floor (the text says p <= 0.01).
- Page text skips from reference 26 (p. 9) to reference 34 (p. 10); references 27-33 are missing from the extraction. No brief claim depends on them.
- 22 athletes, no CIs on r and no power calculation: correlations of about 0.4-0.6 are imprecise.

18	
19	# Collings et al. 2026: Reducing the Risk of ACL Injury With Exercise
20	
21	> **Citation**
22	> Collings TJ, Diamond LE, Barrett RS, Saxby DJ, Lloyd DG, Whiteley R, Patterson BE, Crossley KM, Bourne MN. An Evidence-Based and Mechanistic Approach to Reducing the Risk of Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury: An Exercise and Sport Science Australia Position Statement. Sports Medicine. DOI 10.1007/s40279-026-02450-3 `[p. 1]`
23	>
24	> Year 2026 is printed (accepted 21 April 2026; "The Author(s) 2026") `[p. 1]`. Volume, issue and page numbers are not printed in the text. The Zotero record date (2026-05-14) is not printed in the text.
25	
26	## Why it was promoted
27	
28	Not printed in the text. The Zotero record places the item in the "SecondBrain Queue" collection, which is the only promotion signal available. The statement is written for practitioners who must prescribe ACL injury prevention exercise, and it says existing guidelines do not explain how to make targeted, individual plans `[p. 2]`.
29	
30	## Research question
31	
32	Two aims `[p. 2]`:
33	1. Critically evaluate the effect of existing exercise interventions on ACL injury incidence.
34	2. Synthesise evidence on intrinsic risk factors and mechanistic pathways for non-contact ACL injury, to guide targeted training.
35	
36	## Population and context
37	
38	- Participants: This is a position statement, not a primary study. It draws on published studies of "active individuals" `[p. 2]`. Included trials mostly enrolled female adolescent and young adult team-sport athletes. Ages in Table 1 run from about 13 to 26 years `[Table 1, p. 4]`.
39	- Sport and level: Field and court sports, mainly soccer, basketball and handball. Recreational, high school, college and elite players are represented `[Table 1, p. 4]`. Snow, water-based, police and military populations were excluded from the risk-factor search `[p. 3]`.
40	- Training or return-to-play context: Primary ACL injury prevention. Post-reconstruction athletes are mentioned as a separate high-risk group `[p. 1, p. 12]`.
41	- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Intervention studies needed a separate control group, at least five ACL injuries, and a peer-reviewed journal (conference posters and abstracts excluded) `[p. 2]`. Risk-factor studies needed a prospective or longitudinal cohort design, a non-contact injury mechanism, a field or court sport and at least one significant univariable intrinsic risk factor `[p. 3]`.
42	
43	## Study design and methods
44	
45	- Design: Position statement built on two systematic literature searches in Scopus, Embase and PubMed `[p. 2]`. PRISMA flow diagrams are given for each search `[p. 3]`. One author performed the searches, screening and data extraction `[p. 2]`.
46	- Exposure or intervention: Exercise-based training programs (neuromuscular, warm-up and multi-component) `[p. 2-3]`. Intrinsic risk factors (morphology, biomechanics, neuromuscular, psychological, hormonal, injury history, genetic) `[Table 3, p. 10-11]`.
47	- Comparator: Control groups with no additional training or usual training `[p. 2]`.
48	- Measurements and outcomes: ACL injury incidence, relative risk or relative risk reduction, and PEDro quality scores. Where the original study did not report a relative risk reduction, the authors calculated it from injury rates `[Table 1, p. 4]`. PEDro scores come from previous systematic reviews, using their median, because the authors did not rate the studies themselves `[p. 2]`.
49	- Analysis: Narrative synthesis of trials and cohort studies. Meta-analytic pooled estimates (about 60%) are cited from other published meta-analyses, not from new pooling by the authors `[p. 3]`. The evidence is graded with an adapted Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine scheme `[Table 4, p. 14]`.
50	
51	## Key findings
52	
53	The statement summarises other people's studies. Its findings are the authors' syntheses. Most comparisons are between intervention and control groups in trials, or between people with and without a risk factor. None is a within-person change over time. The results show association and effect on injury rates, not the mechanism behind them, unless the text says so.
54	
55	- Population-level neuromuscular and warm-up programs: meta-analyses indicate about a 60% reduction in ACL injury risk in adolescent female soccer, basketball and handball players, aged 14-18 years `[p. 1]` `[p. 3]`.
56	- Largest cluster RCT (Swedish female adolescent football teams): 64% reduction in all ACL injuries. Based on 7 injuries in 2,479 players (intervention) vs 14 in 2,085 (control). Significant `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
57	- FIFA 11+ cluster RCT in male college soccer players: 76% reduction (3 of 675 vs 16 of 850 injuries). Significant. The authors describe this as the only cluster RCT in males `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
58	- Non-randomised cohort studies report large reductions: PEP in female recreational soccer (82%) and a proprioceptive training study in soccer (87%). Both significant `[Table 1, p. 4]`. The authors describe these designs as at high risk of bias `[p. 6]`.
59	- Of the 12 intervention studies in Table 1, 10 show a reduction in ACL injury risk and 2 show an increase (Knee Ligament Injury Prevention program, 114%; Balance Training, 277%). Only 4 of the 12 report a statistically significant effect `[Table 1, p. 4]`. This count is made from the table for this brief.
60	- Several other intervention studies found reductions that were not statistically significant, which the authors partly attribute to small injury numbers `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
61	- Adherence to injury prevention programs in trial conditions averaged 66 +/- 21% (19 studies) `[p. 6]`.
62	- Female athletes are 3-8 times more likely to sustain an ACL injury than males, depending on the sport `[p. 2]`.
63	- Most ACL injuries occur without contact, during change of direction, lunging or landing from a jump `[p. 8]`. Estimated rupture time is under 50 ms after initial foot contact `[p. 8]`.
64	- Intrinsic risk factors with the most consistent evidence: prior ACL injury (strongest), morphology (smaller ACL size, greater posterior tibial slope, narrower intercondylar notch; mostly non-modifiable), and biomechanical factors (dynamic knee valgus, low knee flexion, lateral trunk flexion, high ground reaction forces) `[p. 9]`.
65	- Neuromuscular strength: a limited number of prospective studies link lower hip or thigh strength to later injury. Current evidence does not show that isokinetic, isometric, concentric or eccentric testing is superior for identifying risk `[p. 9]`.
66	- The authors state that physical testing cannot yet be recommended to identify actionable metrics for reducing ACL injury risk `[p. 12]`. They also state that no externally validated screening test can accurately classify individual risk `[p. 15]`.
67	- Authors' recommendations: Tier 1 (population-level) warm-up programs as the foundation. Level 1 evidence for young female soccer, basketball and handball players `[Table 4, p. 14]`. Tier 2 (targeted, individual) strategies as an adjunct, with direct evidence for reducing injury still limited `[p. 15]`.
68	
69	## Limitations and applicability
70	
71	- Limitations the authors report:
72	  - Most evidence comes from non-randomised or cohort designs at high risk of bias. Half of the studies have fewer than 10 injuries, which can inflate relative risk. Confounder control is limited `[p. 6]`.
73	  - Programs vary widely, from one component to four or more. It is unclear which components drive the effect `[p. 6]`.
74	  - Evidence in males, elite athletes and high-risk sports (for example Australian rules football, netball and rugby) is limited or missing `[p. 6]` `[Table 5, p. 16]`.
75	  - Tier 2 recommendations have not been shown to reduce ACL injury incidence `[p. 15]`.
76	  - No RCT has directly linked a specific exercise to lower injury incidence. Most trials test multi-component programs `[p. 12]`.
77	  - Observational risk factors show associations, not causes, unless confounders are controlled `[p. 11]`. Confounding example: strength and injury risk may both reflect training history `[p. 11]`.
78	  - Biomechanical proxy measures (ground reaction forces, joint moments) may not reflect ligament loading `[p. 13]` `[Table 5, p. 16]`.
79	  - Markerless motion capture is accurate to about 5-10 degrees compared with marker-based systems `[p. 9]`.
80	- Additional transfer limitations (interpretation, not author claims):
81	  - Table 1 pools very different trial designs, ages and sports. A single pooled percentage hides this variation.
82	  - Adherence in real teams is likely below trial adherence, since trial adherence averaged 66% `[p. 6]`.
83	  - Trial results in female adolescents may not carry over to male or adult elite squads.
84	- Reporting issues found on checking the text (this brief's check, not the authors' claims):
85	  - Text gives reductions of 70% for PEP [22] and 29% for FIFA 11 [23]. Table 1 gives 41% and 20% for the same studies `[p. 5]` `[Table 1, p. 4]`.
86	  - Warm-up duration is "10-30 min" in the Abstract and Section 3.2 `[p. 1]` `[p. 6]`, "15-20 min" in Section 6.1 `[p. 14]`, and "20 min or more" in the Level 1 row of Table 4 `[p. 14]`.
87	  - Table 5 is cited in the text at p. 15 but the table itself sits on p. 16. This is a layout detail only.
88	
89	## Practitioner interpretation
90	
91	Interpretation, not a study finding. The authors' Tier 1 advice (warm-up or neuromuscular programs, 2-3 times a week, built on plyometric, strength, balance and agility work) is best supported for young female team-sport athletes `[p. 14]`. For a men's or elite squad, or a sport outside soccer, basketball and handball, the same program is a reasonable default but its effect is less certain `[p. 14]`. Tier 2 drills (landing technique, valgus control, trunk and hip strength) are better treated as selective add-ons for athletes with high exposure to risky tasks or a prior ACL injury `[p. 15]`. Physical screening should not be used to pick who gets targeted work, since the authors say no validated test exists `[p. 15]`. Adherence is a practical limit, so program design should favour short, low-equipment sessions that replace an existing warm-up `[p. 6-7]`.
92	
93	## Evidence map
94	
95	| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
96	|---|---|---|
97	| Neuromuscular or warm-up programs reduce ACL risk by about 60% in young female team-sport athletes (from other meta-analyses) | `[p. 1]` `[p. 3]` | result (cited) |
98	| Largest cluster RCT: 64% reduction, 7/2,479 vs 14/2,085 | `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]` | result |
99	| FIFA 11+ in male college soccer: 76% reduction | `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]` | result |
100	| 10 of 12 intervention studies show a reduction; 4 significant | `[Table 1, p. 4]` | result (counted from table) |
101	| Adherence averaged 66 +/- 21% | `[p. 6]` | result (cited) |
102	| Prior ACL injury is the most consistent risk factor | `[p. 9]` | result (review) |
103	| Risk factors show association, not cause | `[p. 11]` | limitation |
104	| Physical testing cannot yet be recommended for actionable risk reduction | `[p. 12]` | result (authors' conclusion) |
105	| Tier 2 strategies not shown to reduce injury incidence | `[p. 15]` | limitation |
106	| Reduction percentages in text differ from Table 1 | `[p. 5]` `[Table 1, p. 4]` | limitation (reporting) |
107	
108	## Related knowledge
109	
110	- No vault notes are cross-linked yet (`cross-linked: false`).

## Why it was promoted

Not printed in the text. The Zotero record places the item in the "SecondBrain Queue" collection, which is the only promotion signal available. The statement is written for practitioners who must prescribe ACL injury prevention exercise, and it says existing guidelines do not explain how to make targeted, individual plans `[p. 2]`.

## Research question

Two aims `[p. 2]`:
1. Critically evaluate the effect of existing exercise interventions on ACL injury incidence.
2. Synthesise evidence on intrinsic risk factors and mechanistic pathways for non-contact ACL injury, to guide targeted training.

## Population and context

- Participants: This is a position statement, not a primary study. It draws on published studies of "active individuals" `[p. 2]`. Included trials mostly enrolled female adolescent and young adult team-sport athletes. Ages in Table 1 run from about 13 to 26 years `[Table 1, p. 4]`.
- Sport and level: Field and court sports, mainly soccer, basketball and handball. Recreational, high school, college and elite players are represented `[Table 1, p. 4]`. Snow, water-based, police and military populations were excluded from the risk-factor search `[p. 3]`.
- Training or return-to-play context: Primary ACL injury prevention. Post-reconstruction athletes are mentioned as a separate high-risk group `[p. 1, p. 12]`.
- Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Intervention studies needed a separate control group, at least five ACL injuries, and a peer-reviewed journal (conference posters and abstracts excluded) `[p. 2]`. Risk-factor studies needed a prospective or longitudinal cohort design, a non-contact injury mechanism, a field or court sport and at least one significant univariable intrinsic risk factor `[p. 3]`.

## Study design and methods

- Design: Position statement built on two systematic literature searches in Scopus, Embase and PubMed `[p. 2]`. PRISMA flow diagrams are given for each search `[p. 3]`. One author performed the searches, screening and data extraction `[p. 2]`.
- Exposure or intervention: Exercise-based training programs (neuromuscular, warm-up and multi-component) `[p. 2-3]`. Intrinsic risk factors (morphology, biomechanics, neuromuscular, psychological, hormonal, injury history, genetic) `[Table 3, p. 10-11]`.
- Comparator: Control groups with no additional training or usual training `[p. 2]`.
- Measurements and outcomes: ACL injury incidence, relative risk or relative risk reduction, and PEDro quality scores. Where the original study did not report a relative risk reduction, the authors calculated it from injury rates `[Table 1, p. 4]`. PEDro scores come from previous systematic reviews, using their median, because the authors did not rate the studies themselves `[p. 2]`.
- Analysis: Narrative synthesis of trials and cohort studies. Meta-analytic pooled estimates (about 60%) are cited from other published meta-analyses, not from new pooling by the authors `[p. 3]`. The evidence is graded with an adapted Oxford Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine scheme `[Table 4, p. 14]`.

## Key findings

The statement summarises other people's studies. Its findings are the authors' syntheses. Most comparisons are between intervention and control groups in trials, or between people with and without a risk factor. None is a within-person change over time. The results show association and effect on injury rates, not the mechanism behind them, unless the text says so.

- Population-level neuromuscular and warm-up programs: meta-analyses indicate about a 60% reduction in ACL injury risk in adolescent female soccer, basketball and handball players, aged 14-18 years `[p. 1]` `[p. 3]`.
- Largest cluster RCT (Swedish female adolescent football teams): 64% reduction in all ACL injuries. Based on 7 injuries in 2,479 players (intervention) vs 14 in 2,085 (control). Significant `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
- FIFA 11+ cluster RCT in male college soccer players: 76% reduction (3 of 675 vs 16 of 850 injuries). Significant. The authors describe this as the only cluster RCT in males `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
- Non-randomised cohort studies report large reductions: PEP in female recreational soccer (82%) and a proprioceptive training study in soccer (87%). Both significant `[Table 1, p. 4]`. The authors describe these designs as at high risk of bias `[p. 6]`.
- Of the 12 intervention studies in Table 1, 10 show a reduction in ACL injury risk and 2 show an increase (Knee Ligament Injury Prevention program, 114%; Balance Training, 277%). Only 4 of the 12 report a statistically significant effect `[Table 1, p. 4]`. This count is made from the table for this brief.
- Several other intervention studies found reductions that were not statistically significant, which the authors partly attribute to small injury numbers `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]`.
- Adherence to injury prevention programs in trial conditions averaged 66 +/- 21% (19 studies) `[p. 6]`.
- Female athletes are 3-8 times more likely to sustain an ACL injury than males, depending on the sport `[p. 2]`.
- Most ACL injuries occur without contact, during change of direction, lunging or landing from a jump `[p. 8]`. Estimated rupture time is under 50 ms after initial foot contact `[p. 8]`.
- Intrinsic risk factors with the most consistent evidence: prior ACL injury (strongest), morphology (smaller ACL size, greater posterior tibial slope, narrower intercondylar notch; mostly non-modifiable), and biomechanical factors (dynamic knee valgus, low knee flexion, lateral trunk flexion, high ground reaction forces) `[p. 9]`.
- Neuromuscular strength: a limited number of prospective studies link lower hip or thigh strength to later injury. Current evidence does not show that isokinetic, isometric, concentric or eccentric testing is superior for identifying risk `[p. 9]`.
- The authors state that physical testing cannot yet be recommended to identify actionable metrics for reducing ACL injury risk `[p. 12]`. They also state that no externally validated screening test can accurately classify individual risk `[p. 15]`.
- Authors' recommendations: Tier 1 (population-level) warm-up programs as the foundation. Level 1 evidence for young female soccer, basketball and handball players `[Table 4, p. 14]`. Tier 2 (targeted, individual) strategies as an adjunct, with direct evidence for reducing injury still limited `[p. 15]`.

## Limitations and applicability

- Limitations the authors report:
  - Most evidence comes from non-randomised or cohort designs at high risk of bias. Half of the studies have fewer than 10 injuries, which can inflate relative risk. Confounder control is limited `[p. 6]`.
  - Programs vary widely, from one component to four or more. It is unclear which components drive the effect `[p. 6]`.
  - Evidence in males, elite athletes and high-risk sports (for example Australian rules football, netball and rugby) is limited or missing `[p. 6]` `[Table 5, p. 16]`.
  - Tier 2 recommendations have not been shown to reduce ACL injury incidence `[p. 15]`.
  - No RCT has directly linked a specific exercise to lower injury incidence. Most trials test multi-component programs `[p. 12]`.
  - Observational risk factors show associations, not causes, unless confounders are controlled `[p. 11]`. Confounding example: strength and injury risk may both reflect training history `[p. 11]`.
  - Biomechanical proxy measures (ground reaction forces, joint moments) may not reflect ligament loading `[p. 13]` `[Table 5, p. 16]`.
  - Markerless motion capture is accurate to about 5-10 degrees compared with marker-based systems `[p. 9]`.
- Additional transfer limitations (interpretation, not author claims):
  - Table 1 pools very different trial designs, ages and sports. A single pooled percentage hides this variation.
  - Adherence in real teams is likely below trial adherence, since trial adherence averaged 66% `[p. 6]`.
  - Trial results in female adolescents may not carry over to male or adult elite squads.
- Reporting issues found on checking the text (this brief's check, not the authors' claims):
  - Text gives reductions of 70% for PEP [22] and 29% for FIFA 11 [23]. Table 1 gives 41% and 20% for the same studies `[p. 5]` `[Table 1, p. 4]`.
  - Warm-up duration is "10-30 min" in the Abstract and Section 3.2 `[p. 1]` `[p. 6]`, "15-20 min" in Section 6.1 `[p. 14]`, and "20 min or more" in the Level 1 row of Table 4 `[p. 14]`.
  - Table 5 is cited in the text at p. 15 but the table itself sits on p. 16. This is a layout detail only.

## Practitioner interpretation

Interpretation, not a study finding. The authors' Tier 1 advice (warm-up or neuromuscular programs, 2-3 times a week, built on plyometric, strength, balance and agility work) is best supported for young female team-sport athletes `[p. 14]`. For a men's or elite squad, or a sport outside soccer, basketball and handball, the same program is a reasonable default but its effect is less certain `[p. 14]`. Tier 2 drills (landing technique, valgus control, trunk and hip strength) are better treated as selective add-ons for athletes with high exposure to risky tasks or a prior ACL injury `[p. 15]`. Physical screening should not be used to pick who gets targeted work, since the authors say no validated test exists `[p. 15]`. Adherence is a practical limit, so program design should favour short, low-equipment sessions that replace an existing warm-up `[p. 6-7]`.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Neuromuscular or warm-up programs reduce ACL risk by about 60% in young female team-sport athletes (from other meta-analyses) | `[p. 1]` `[p. 3]` | result (cited) |
| Largest cluster RCT: 64% reduction, 7/2,479 vs 14/2,085 | `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]` | result |
| FIFA 11+ in male college soccer: 76% reduction | `[Table 1, p. 4]` `[p. 5]` | result |
| 10 of 12 intervention studies show a reduction; 4 significant | `[Table 1, p. 4]` | result (counted from table) |
| Adherence averaged 66 +/- 21% | `[p. 6]` | result (cited) |
| Prior ACL injury is the most consistent risk factor | `[p. 9]` | result (review) |
| Risk factors show association, not cause | `[p. 11]` | limitation |
| Physical testing cannot yet be recommended for actionable risk reduction | `[p. 12]` | result (authors' conclusion) |
| Tier 2 strategies not shown to reduce injury incidence | `[p. 15]` | limitation |
| Reduction percentages in text differ from Table 1 | `[p. 5]` `[Table 1, p. 4]` | limitation (reporting) |

14	Abstract
15	Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is a serious sporting injury associated with impaired performance, high recurrence 
16	rates, early-onset knee osteoarthritis and substantial health and economic burden. In Australia, ACL injury incidence has 
17	increased over the past two decades, with particularly high rates observed among female and adolescent athletes participat-
18	ing in cutting and landing sports. Neuromuscular and structured warm-up programs can reduce ACL injury risk; however, 
19	implementation and adherence remain inconsistent, and evidence for effectiveness in males, elite athletes and several high-risk 
20	sports is unclear. Practitioners, therefore, require clear, evidence-based guidance to prescribe effective prevention strategies 
21	across diverse populations. This position statement provides contemporary, evidence-informed recommendations to guide 
22	exercise prescription for ACL injury prevention by (1) critically evaluating the effect of existing exercise interventions on 
23	ACL injury incidence, and (2) synthesising evidence on intrinsic risk factors and mechanistic pathways for non-contact 
24	ACL injury to inform targeted training strategies. Two systematic literature searches were conducted in Scopus, Embase 
25	and PubMed. The first identified randomised and non-randomised controlled trials and cohort studies evaluating the effect 
26	of exercise-based interventions on ACL injury incidence. The second identified prospective studies examining intrinsic risk 
27	factors for non-contact ACL injury. Evidence on ACL injury aetiology was synthesised by integrating injury risk factors, 
28	video analyses of injury events, in vivo and in vitro laboratory studies and in silico biomechanical modelling. We propose a 
29	tiered framework for exercise prescription. Tier 1 strategies emphasise population-level neuromuscular and structured warm-
30	up programs, which meta-analyses indicate can reduce ACL injury risk by approximately 60% in adolescent female soccer, 
31	basketball and handball players. Effective programs typically combine plyometric, strength, balance/proprioception, mobility 
32	and agility exercises performed for 10–30 min, 2–3 times per week. Tier 2 strategies target specific neuromuscular deficits 
33	or high-risk movement patterns, including low knee flexion, dynamic knee valgus, lateral trunk flexion and excessive step 
34	width. Interventions may include plyometric and resistance exercises, motor control drills and neurocognitive challenges to 
35	increase transfer to game scenarios; however, direct evidence linking Tier 2 strategies to reduced injury incidence remains 
36	limited. This position statement provides an evidence-based framework to support the design and practical implementation 
37	of effective ACL injury prevention strategies in sport. 
38	1  Background
39	Anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) rupture is a devastating 
40	sporting injury and Australia has the highest rate of ACL 
41	reconstruction surgery in the world (77.4 per 100,000) [1]. 
42	After returning to sports following ACL reconstruction, 
43	many athletes are unable to achieve their pre-injury level 
44	of performance [2] and often display pronounced deficits 
45	in muscle strength [3], power [4] and size [5], in addition 
46	to reduced psychological well-being [6]. Up to one-third of 
47	athletes then go on to sustain a second ACL rupture, either 
48	to the same or opposite knee, resulting in further time loss 
49	and increased likelihood of ceasing sports participation alto-
50	gether [7]. Long-term, ACL injury also results in an elevated 
51	risk of early-onset knee osteoarthritis [8, 9]. Collectively, 
52	these adverse outcomes impose a significant health and eco-
53	nomic burden [10].
54	Despite a proliferation of research, male and female
